site.label: Home
site.text: Wadduwage Lab. Next-generation imaging for biology. We work at the intersection of biophotonics, computational imaging, and deep learning to design the microscopes of the future.

site.label: Research
site.text: Every biological image is a measurement shaped by optics and computation. We treat the whole chain, from the photons leaving a sample to the conclusion a scientist draws, as one system that can be designed, learned and checked.

site.label: Research · Differentiable microscopy
site.text: Research thrust "Differentiable microscopy": Optics designed by machine learning. Most microscopes are still designed optics first: lenses form a sharp picture, and computation is added afterward. We ask what happens when the optics themselves are learned. By modeling how light travels through a material, we train a physical element the way we train a neural network, then fabricate it with collaborators at nanometer precision. These three-dimensional structures work in visible light and are designed to process an image as light passes through them. Our long-term goal is microscopes designed end to end for the biological question they answer, with part of the computation done by the light itself. Key papers: QuATON · Optics Express 2026 (https://doi.org/10.1364/OE.546074); 3D nanoprecise metastructures, with the Boyden and So labs · Nature Photonics 2026 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41566-026-01896-1); Volumetric diffractive networks · arXiv 2026 (preprint) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07896); Towards ultrafast quantitative phase imaging · Biomedical Optics Express 2024 (https://doi.org/10.1364/BOE.504954).

site.label: Research · DEEP · de-scattering with excitation patterning
site.text: Research thrust "DEEP · de-scattering with excitation patterning": Imaging deep inside living tissue. Cells deep inside living tissue are hard to see because light scatters there, like headlights in fog. Our DEEP methods use multiphoton excitation to light up a whole plane at once, encode it with patterns of light, and recover a sharp image from the scattered signal with computation. Neural networks made DEEP an order of magnitude faster (DEEP²), and we are now making these reconstructions learn from the physics of each experiment instead of from large training sets. The aim is to watch cells, including synapses in the living brain, in their native environment and fast enough to follow what they do. Key papers: DEEP · Science Advances 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aay5496); DEEP² · Light: Science & Applications 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41377-023-01248-6); Untrained networks for structured illumination · Chemical & Biomedical Imaging 2026 (https://doi.org/10.1021/cbmi.5c00153).

site.label: Research · Bias · uncertainty · validity
site.text: Research thrust "Bias · uncertainty · validity": Trustworthy machine learning for biomedicine. Anything learned from data can inherit its biases, be it a neural network or a learned optical element. A model can score well yet fail on samples unlike its training set, or learn how the data were collected instead of the biology. We develop methods to understand, test and mitigate these biases in the optics and algorithms we build, such as uncertainty estimates that show where a model is unsure and statistical tests that check whether a reported accuracy reflects real signal. We apply them to digital pathology and to diagnosing infections and antimicrobial resistance, with collaborators in Norway, India and Sri Lanka. Key papers: Beyond Perfect Scores · arXiv 2026 (preprint) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06704); Uncertainty-aware labeling in digital pathology · WACV 2025 (https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61041.2025.00067); Phase microscopy and genome sequencing for resistance detection · Frontiers in Microbiology 2023 (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2023.1154620); SERS nanowire chip for resistant bacteria · ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.3c00612).

site.label: Research · foundations
site.text: The lab's approach grew out of earlier instruments whose optics were designed around their reconstruction algorithms. They include a 3D image cytometer that imaged about 800 cells per second, recognized with the Cytometry Part A 2015 best paper award, and a compressive hyperspectral imager (Optica 2017).

site.label: Resources
site.text: Resources page for prospective and incoming students (reviewed Oct 2026). A starting point for students who are thinking about joining the lab or have just been admitted. It collects what we ask new members to read, run and practice in their first weeks, so that you can begin before you arrive. Work through it at your own pace.

site.label: Resources · start
site.text: Read three short stories about our work: 30 min Plain-language introductions to two of the lab's directions: imaging through scattering tissue, and optics designed by machine learning. DEEP²: (https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2023/10/a-deeper-squared-dive-into-ai/) DEEP: (https://news.mit.edu/2021/microscopy-tissue-images-0707) 3D metastructures: (https://news.mit.edu/2026/powerful-shrinking-technique-could-enable-devices-compute-light-0512) Learn the vocabulary: 15 min The glossary at the end of this page defines the terms you will hear in lab meetings. Glossary: (#glossary) Run a differentiable microscope: 2 h Open the Colab notebooks of our all-optical phase-retrieval paper and train an optical system end to end in your browser. All-Optical-QPM: (https://github.com/wadduwagelab/All-Optical-QPM) Listen to Tensor & Bias: 8 episodes The podcast of our deep learning course, one AI-narrated episode per module, from tensors and GPUs to how models fail in the wild. Spotify: (https://open.spotify.com/show/033Aem6pMGVLeZftOmAEFj) Start Writing in the Sciences: module 1, ≈2 h Kristin Sainani's free Stanford course. New members are asked to take it, and the lab's internal writing handbook is based on it. Course: (https://www.coursera.org/learn/sciwrite) Videos: (https://www.youtube.com/@sciwritestanford1636)

site.label: Resources · apply
site.text: PhD students join the lab through the graduate programs at Old Dominion University. Current students are in the PhD program in Computer Science; students from Physics and Data Science are also welcome. Admission decisions are made by the graduate programs, so apply to the program as well as writing to the lab. Check the program's application deadline early; deadlines for international applicants are often earlier. ODU M.S. and undergraduate students who would like research experience are also welcome to write. Linear algebra and some calculus and probability. Programming in Python (NumPy; PyTorch or JAX is a plus). Some exposure to optics, signal or image processing, or machine learning. You do not need all three; the learning path below fills the gaps. Curiosity about biology. The lab builds instruments and methods for biologists and clinicians. Read two or three of our papers (see Read our work (#papers)) and decide which direction interests you most. Email Dushan Wadduwage with your CV, the direction you are interested in and why, and one of our papers you read, with a question or idea about it. A subject line such as "Prospective PhD student: differentiable microscopy" helps. Apply to the ODU graduate program by its deadline and name the lab in your statement.

site.label: Resources · path
site.text: About ten to twelve weeks at eight to ten hours a week for a student with an engineering or physics background. Do the foundations first, then run the deep learning track in parallel with optics and computational imaging, and finish with the reading on multiphoton microscopy. If time is short, do the items marked core. Items marked our course are assigned in the lab's own courses at ODU. International students: start the visa steps in Joining ODU (#arrival) first; appointments can take weeks. Self-check exercises adapted from assignments in the lab's courses. Do them in a Colab notebook and share it with Dushan before your first one-on-one meeting.

site.label: Resources · path

Brady, University of Arizona (companion to his textbook) (https://github.com/arizonaCameraLab/computationalImaging) Code 10 h (assigned in the lab's courses) Single-pixel imaging via compressive sampling: by Duarte et al., IEEE Signal Processing Magazine (2008) (https://doi.org/10.1109/MSP.2007.914730) Paper 1 h. site.label: Resources · path
site.text: Multiphoton and temporal-focusing microscopy: Weeks 11–12 Background for the DEEP family of instruments. Read these before the lab's own DEEP papers. Two-photon laser scanning fluorescence microscopy: by Denk, Strickler and Webb, Science (1990) (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.2321027) Paper 1 h (do this first) Deep tissue two-photon microscopy: by Helmchen and Denk, Nature Methods (2005) (https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth818) Review 2 h. Scanningless depth-resolved microscopy: by Oron, Tal and Silberberg, Optics Express (2005) (https://doi.org/10.1364/OPEX.13.001468) Paper 1 h. Simultaneous spatial and temporal focusing of femtosecond pulses: by Zhu et al., Optics Express (2005) (https://doi.org/10.1364/OPEX.13.002153) Paper 1 h. Scanless two-photon excitation with temporal focusing: by Papagiakoumou, Ronzitti and Emiliani, Nature Methods (2020) (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-020-0795-y) Review 2 h. Sampling: CS 795/895 ≈3 h Sample a 1D signal and then a 2D image above, at and below the Nyquist rate, reconstruct them, and explain the aliasing you see. Noise and denoising: CS 795/895 ≈10 h Write a forward model with Poisson (shot) and Gaussian (read) noise for a fluorescence image, then train one supervised and one self-supervised denoiser (in the spirit of Noise2Void (https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.10980)) and compare them.

site.text: Fourier features: CS 740/840 ≈10 h Reproduce Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10739) (Tancik et al., 2020). Sweep depth, width, learning rate and the size of the Fourier mapping, then replace the MLP with a CNN. Architecture audit: DASC 428/528 ≈2 h Take a small CNN written for 28×28 grayscale images and adapt it to CIFAR-10. Recompute every tensor shape and the parameter count by hand before you run it.

site.label: Resources · papers
site.text: Three to five papers per research direction, in the order we suggest reading them. Start with the direction you are most likely to work on, then read the first paper of each of the others. Optics designed by machine learning: Differentiable microscopy Towards ultrafast quantitative phase imaging via differentiable microscopy · Biomedical Optics Express 2024: (https://doi.org/10.1364/BOE.504954) A worked example of learning the optics and the reconstruction together. Differentiable microscopy designs an all optical phase retrieval microscope · arXiv 2022: (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14944) The next step: the light does all of the computation. Pairs with the Colab notebooks. QuATON: quantization aware training of optical neurons · Optics Express 2026: (https://doi.org/10.1364/OE.546074) How learned optical elements survive the limits of fabrication. 3D nanoprecise metastructures, with the Boyden and So labs · Nature Photonics 2026: (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41566-026-01896-1) A fabrication route for the 3D optical structures that learned designs need. Beyond the thin-layer limit: volumetric diffractive networks · arXiv 2026: (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07896) Advanced: differentiable beam propagation for thick optical networks.

site.label: Resources · papers
site.text: Imaging deep inside living tissue: DEEP · de-scattering with excitation patterning DEEP · Science Advances 2021: (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aay5496) The founding paper: patterned excitation and computation to image through scattering. DEEP² · Light: Science & Applications 2023: (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41377-023-01248-6) A neural network makes DEEP about ten times faster. Code and data are public. mosTF microscopy for in vivo brain imaging · Scientific Reports 2024: (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-57208-6) A related optical approach to scattering, with the So and Nedivi labs. Untrained networks for structured illumination · Chemical & Biomedical Imaging 2026: (https://doi.org/10.1021/cbmi.5c00153) Reconstruction that learns from the physics of one experiment instead of a training set. Motion-guided sparse correction for microscopy point tracking · arXiv 2026: (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29220) Following moving cells in microscopy video, with a browser demo.

site.label: Resources · papers
site.text: Trustworthy machine learning for biomedicine: Bias · uncertainty · validity Thinking in groups: permutation tests reveal near-out-of-distribution · arXiv 2024: (https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14058) A gentle introduction to testing models on groups of samples. Beyond Perfect Scores: proof-by-contradiction for trustworthy ML · arXiv 2026: (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06704) The core method: does a reported accuracy reflect real signal? Code is public. Uncertainty-aware labeling in digital pathology · WACV 2025: (https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61041.2025.00067) Uncertainty estimates put to work in pathology. Phase microscopy and genome sequencing for resistance detection · Frontiers in Microbiology 2023: (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2023.1154620) The application domain: antimicrobial resistance.

site.text: Public repositories that are good first exercises, easiest first. Getting a published result to run on your own machine is the fastest way to learn a codebase. site.label: Resources · glossary
site.text: Computational imaging: Imaging in which the final picture is computed from raw measurements rather than formed directly by lenses. Differentiable microscopy (∂µ): Modeling the optics and the reconstruction as one differentiable system, so that both can be trained together by backpropagation. Forward model / inverse problem: The forward model predicts the measurement from the sample; the inverse problem recovers the sample from a measurement that the optics have blurred, scattered or encoded. Scattering: Light changing direction many times inside tissue, like headlights in fog. It blurs images taken deep in tissue. Multiphoton (two-photon) excitation: Fluorescence excited only where the laser intensity is very high, which confines the signal and lets microscopes image deeper. TFM: Temporal focusing microscopy: wide-field multiphoton imaging that excites a whole plane at once by focusing the laser pulse in time. Structured illumination (SIM): Illuminating the sample with known patterns so that computation can recover information that a single image loses. DEEP: De-scattering with excitation patterning: patterned temporal-focusing excitation plus a computational reconstruction to see through scattering. DEEP²: DEEP with a neural network that needs far fewer patterns, making imaging about ten times faster.

site.label: Resources · glossary
site.text: QPI / QPM: Quantitative phase imaging (microscopy): label-free imaging of how much a transparent cell delays light, which relates to its thickness and density. D2NN: Diffractive deep neural network: stacked optical layers whose structure is learned so that light passing through them computes. Optical neuron: A single learnable element of a diffractive network, for example the phase delay of one pixel. BPM / ∂BPM: The beam propagation method, a model of light propagating through a medium; ∂BPM is its differentiable version, used to train thick optical networks. FDTD: Finite-difference time-domain: a full-wave simulation of light used to check that faster, simpler models are accurate. Untrained network: A neural network fitted to a single measurement with the physics built in, without a training set. Out-of-distribution (OOD): Data unlike the data a model was trained on, where its predictions should not be trusted. Permutation test: A statistical test that shuffles labels to check whether a result could have arisen by chance.

papers.title: Beyond the Thin-Layer Limit: Differentiable Volumetric Training for Visible-Range Diffractive Neural Networks

abstract.text: Diffractive deep neural networks ($D^{2}$NNs) promise miniaturized power-efficient, light-speed optical front-ends for machine vision, yet the most mature demonstrations remain in the terahertz regime, built from readily fabricated millimeter-scale neurons. Translating $D^{2}$NNs to the visible range—where nearly all vision pipelines operate—was long blamed on the difficulty of fabricating nanoscale neurons; but even after recent advances removed that barrier, visible-range $D^{2}$NNs matching their terahertz counterparts remain out of reach. We identify the true obstacle as the thin-layer approximation underlying nearly all $D^{2}$NN training, which treats each diffractive layer as an infinitely thin mask. It fails not because of the short wavelength, as is commonly assumed, but because the low-refractive-index materials ($n\approx 1.3$–$1.5$) used at visible wavelengths require relief structures thick enough that intra-layer diffraction and phase accumulation become significant. To overcome this, we introduce a differentiable beam-propagation ($\partial$BPM) layer that models each element as a finite-thickness volume and propagates light through it during training, keeping the fabrication-compatible height map end-to-end trainable without full-wave simulation in the loop. Across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-100 classification and imaging, $\partial$BPM training substantially reduces the design-to-device mismatch, and full-wave FDTD validation raises classification accuracy from $50\%$ to $90\%$ without re-optimization. The $\partial$BPM layer thus offers a scalable, physics-aware bridge between efficient optical neural-network optimization and fabrication-consistent diffractive design.

papers.title: Motion-guided sparse correction enables expert-quality point tracking across diverse microscopy regimes
papers.authors: Zimianitis, L., Thenahandi, P., Buckhalter, K., Jayakody, D., Kimura, J. O., Liang, X., Cunningham, K., Ahmad, A., Ahluwalia, B. S., Jayarathna, S., Chrisochoides, N., Weissbourd, B., & Wadduwage, D. N.

abstract.text: Tracking the dynamics of non-canonical biological systems in microscopy videos remains a persistent challenge. Both classical and learning-based trackers depend on expert-reviewed data to be evaluated and adapted, yet exhaustive manual annotation rarely scales to the videos where these tools are needed most. We developed RIPPLE (Refinement Interpolation Platform for Point Location Estimation), which recasts annotation as sparse correction: a user clicks a starting point, RIPPLE proposes a full trajectory, and the user intervenes only where the trajectory drifts. We tested RIPPLE on five challenging microscopy datasets from our laboratories, four from the transparent jellyfish Clytia hemisphaerica and one tracking landmarks on rapidly moving sperm. Across these, RIPPLE matched the quality of exhaustive manual annotation while reducing manual clicks by 3 to 25 times across datasets. RIPPLE thereby fills a missing layer between manual annotation and fully automated tracking, enabling immediate quantification of biological dynamics, method benchmarking, and the production of the gold-standard data needed to adapt future automated microscopy trackers.

papers.title: Beyond Perfect Scores: Proof-by-Contradiction for Trustworthy Machine Learning
papers.authors: Wadduwage, D. N.*, Jayakody, D., & Zimianitis, L.

abstract.text: Machine learning (ML) models show strong promise for new biomedical prediction tasks, but concerns about trustworthiness have hindered their clinical adoption. In particular, it is often unclear whether a model relies on true clinical cues or on spurious hierarchical correlations in the data. This paper introduces a simple yet broadly applicable trustworthiness test grounded in stochastic proof-by-contradiction. Instead of just showing high test performance, our approach trains and tests on spurious labels carefully permuted based on a potential outcomes framework. A truly trustworthy model should fail under such label permutation; comparable accuracy across real and permuted labels indicates overfitting, shortcut learning, or data leakage. Our approach quantifies this behavior through interpretable Fisher-style $p$-values, which are well understood by domain experts across medical and life sciences. We evaluate our approach on multiple new bacterial diagnostics to separate tasks and models learning genuine causal relationships from those driven by dataset artifacts or statistical coincidences. Our work establishes a foundation to build rigor and trust between ML and life-science research communities, moving ML models one step closer to clinical adoption.

papers.title: Thinking in Groups: Permutation Tests Reveal Near-Out-of-Distribution
papers.authors: Jayawardana, Y., Jayakody, D., Jayarathna, S., & Wadduwage, D. N.

abstract.text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have the potential to power many biomedical workflows, but training them on truly representative, IID datasets is often infeasible. Most models instead rely on biased or incomplete data, making them prone to out-of-distribution (OoD) inputs that closely resemble in-distribution samples. Such near-OoD cases are harder to detect than standard OOD benchmarks and can cause unreliable—even catastrophic—predictions. Biomedical assays, however, offer a unique opportunity: they often generate multiple correlated measurements per specimen through biological or technical replicates. Exploiting this insight, we introduce Homogeneous OoD (HOoD), a novel OoD detection framework for correlated data. HOoD projects groups of correlated measurements through a trained model and uses permutation-based hypothesis tests to compare them with known subpopulations. Each test yields an interpretable p-value, quantifying how well a group matches a subpopulation. By aggregating these p-values, HOoD reliably identifies OoD groups. In evaluations, HOoD consistently outperforms point-wise and ensemble-based OoD detectors, demonstrating its promise for robust real-world deployment.
